title: Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment (UK Guide)

content:
Quick answer: Inflammatory arthritis describes conditions involving inflammation in joints and sometimes the spine or tendon attachments, including rheumatoid, psoriatic and reactive arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis. Symptoms and treatments vary. Persistent swelling needs assessment, and normal blood tests do not rule every condition out. A sudden very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent help.

What is inflammatory arthritis?

Inflammatory arthritis is a broad description, not one diagnosis. It includes conditions in which inflammation affects joints, the spine or the places where tendons and ligaments attach to bone. Immune-system activity is involved in several of these conditions, but their causes, patterns and treatment are not identical.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune condition that often affects joints in the hands, feet and wrists. It can also affect other parts of the body.
  • Psoriatic arthritis can affect joints, fingers or toes, nails and tendon attachments. It is associated with psoriasis, but joint symptoms still need checking if you do not have an obvious skin rash.
  • Axial spondyloarthritis mainly affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. Ankylosing spondylitis is a form with changes visible on X-ray. Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis may not show those X-ray changes.
  • Reactive arthritis can develop after an infection, often involving the gut or urinary or genital tract. It often settles within about six months, although it can last longer or come back.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a related inflammatory condition, not another name for these joint diseases. It mainly causes pain and stiffness around the shoulders, neck and hips, usually in people over 50. Its assessment and steroid treatment differ, so it should not be folded into a single DMARD treatment plan.

How is it different from osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis involves changes in joint tissues, including cartilage, and can also cause swelling. It is not simply inevitable wear from using a joint. Activity-related pain and no morning stiffness, or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes, can support an osteoarthritis diagnosis in the right setting. NICE NG226, recommendation 1.1.1, applies that clinical pattern to people aged 45 or over.

Longer morning stiffness, persistent swelling, back pain that improves with movement, swollen fingers or toes, psoriasis, or eye inflammation may suggest an inflammatory condition. None proves a diagnosis alone, and not everyone has the same pattern. Symptoms can overlap. Exercise remains an important part of care for many conditions; pain with activity is not a reason to assume that all movement is damaging.

Symptoms worth discussing with a GP

  • new or persistent joint pain, swelling or stiffness
  • difficulty getting moving after rest, especially prolonged morning stiffness
  • swollen fingers or toes, or persistent pain where a tendon attaches to bone
  • persistent back pain, particularly if it started before age 45, wakes you at night or improves with movement
  • fatigue, psoriasis or nail changes, or symptoms involving the eyes, skin, bowel or urinary tract

You do not need every symptom, symmetrical joint symptoms or a particular stiffness duration to ask for assessment. NICE NG65, recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.6, warns against ruling out spondyloarthritis on one sign, symptom or test. Its axial referral criteria need a clinician's assessment; this is not a self-diagnosis checklist.

Diagnosis and referral: do not wait for abnormal blood tests

A clinician considers your history and examines the affected areas. Tests may include blood tests, imaging or joint-fluid testing, depending on the suspected cause. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are relevant to suspected RA; they are not universal tests for every inflammatory condition. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude all inflammatory arthritis, and seronegative disease is not the same as having no inflammation.

NICE NG100, recommendation 1.1.1, says any adult with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause should be referred for specialist opinion. Referral should be urgent if small hand or foot joints or more than one joint are affected, or if there has been a delay of three months or longer before seeking advice, even with normal inflammatory markers or negative rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP. Investigations should not delay referral. The three-month criterion is not an instruction to wait.

For suspected new-onset inflammatory arthritis in the spondyloarthritis pathway, NG65, recommendation 1.1.8, calls for urgent rheumatology referral, with different pathways if RA, gout or acute calcium pyrophosphate arthritis is suspected. Recommendations 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 say negative HLA-B27 or normal CRP and ESR do not rule out spondyloarthritis. A normal X-ray also does not exclude non-radiographic axial disease.

Early assessment and appropriate treatment can reduce the risk of long-term problems. There is no single damage timeline that applies to every condition or person.

Treatment depends on the diagnosis

There is no one treatment sequence for all inflammatory arthritis. Your team balances symptoms, inflammation, other health conditions, medicine risks and your preferences. Do not start, stop or increase prescribed medicines using this guide.

  • RA: NICE NG100 recommends early conventional DMARD treatment for newly diagnosed active RA, ideally within three months of persistent symptoms. The treatment target is remission or low disease activity. Further conventional, biological or targeted synthetic DMARD treatment depends on response and the relevant criteria. Short-term glucocorticoid bridging may be considered when starting a new conventional DMARD; this is not a long-term steroid plan for everyone.
  • Psoriatic and other peripheral inflammatory arthritis: treatment may include NSAIDs, local steroid injections, conventional DMARDs or biological or targeted treatments, according to the pattern and severity. Skin disease and other affected areas also matter.
  • Axial spondyloarthritis: NICE NG65 recommends an NSAID for associated pain at the lowest effective dose with risk assessment and monitoring. Specialist exercise and physiotherapy are important. Biological or targeted treatments may be options if the disease remains active and eligibility criteria are met. Conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate are not a general treatment for spinal symptoms; they may be used for inflammation in other joints.
  • Reactive arthritis: treatment may include anti-inflammatory medicines and physiotherapy. Antibiotics are used if the triggering infection is still present, not as an automatic treatment for every episode. Persistent disease may need specialist medicines.
  • PMR: prednisolone is the main treatment and often needs a gradual reduction over a prolonged course under medical supervision. Do not stop prescribed steroids suddenly.

NSAIDs can reduce pain and inflammation; they are not merely pain-masking medicines. They do not replace disease-modifying treatment when that is needed. Suitability depends on factors such as stomach, kidney and cardiovascular risk, interactions and pregnancy. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist rather than assuming an over-the-counter option is safe for you.

Relevant treatment sources include NG100 recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.4.1 to 1.4.3, NG65 sections 1.4 and 1.5 and the NHS condition pages listed below. These are condition-specific recommendations, not NICE approval of this article.

Living with symptoms and getting support

A plan may include suitable exercise, pacing, a symptom diary, sleep and fatigue support, and adjustments to daily tasks or work. Balance activity and rest with advice matched to your condition. Do not push through a sudden hot, swollen or very painful joint while waiting to see if exercise helps.

NICE NG100 supports access to specialist physiotherapy, occupational therapy when daily tasks or hand function are affected, and podiatry for foot problems. NG65 recommends an individualised, structured exercise programme with a specialist physiotherapist for axial spondyloarthritis, and therapist support for difficulties with everyday activities. Ask who coordinates your care, how to get advice between appointments and what your flare plan should cover.

Outlook varies. Many people with RA have substantial periods between flares with appropriate treatment. Axial disease has a variable course, and reactive arthritis may resolve rather than become lifelong. Remission is a treatment aim for RA, not a promise that most people with every inflammatory condition will have the same course.

When to get urgent or emergency help

A sudden very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without a fever. It may be an infection or another acute condition, not an ordinary flare. NHS septic arthritis advice says symptoms need checking straight away. Fever, shivering or feeling unwell during immune-suppressing treatment also needs prompt advice; do not label this a flare without assessment.

Eye pain, redness, light sensitivity or blurred vision needs urgent assessment. NICE NG65, recommendation 1.1.12, calls for immediate same-day ophthalmological assessment when acute anterior uveitis is suspected. Use an urgent GP, optometrist or eye-service route to arrange care. NHS uveitis advice says loss of vision needs A&E or 999. Do not wait for your next routine rheumatology appointment.

If you have PMR or suspected PMR, a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when eating or talking, or visual symptoms can indicate giant cell arteritis. Seek urgent medical help; visual symptoms need same-day eye assessment. Sudden loss of vision is an emergency.

For urgent non-emergency help in England, Scotland or Wales, ask for an urgent GP appointment or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency, such as severe breathing difficulty, collapse or sudden confusion during a possible infection. Follow any specific infection instructions supplied by your clinical team.

Frequently asked questions

Is inflammatory arthritis the same as RA?

No. RA is one type. Psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis and reactive arthritis have different patterns and may need different treatment. PMR is a related inflammatory condition with a different main presentation.

Can blood tests rule it out?

No single blood test rules out every inflammatory condition. Normal inflammatory markers or negative antibodies must be interpreted alongside symptoms and examination, and should not delay a referral that is needed.

Is it always lifelong?

Many conditions are long term, but reactive arthritis often settles within about six months. Symptoms, flares and long-term outlook vary. Ask your team what applies to your diagnosis rather than assuming one prognosis for all types.

Can it run in families?

Family history or genetic factors can increase the likelihood of some conditions, but they do not establish a diagnosis. A positive or negative HLA-B27 result alone cannot confirm or exclude spondyloarthritis.

Educational information only, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan. Seek clinical assessment for new or changing symptoms and follow advice from your own team.
